profile.summary: Job presents the drama of a just one who suffers without his suffering being explainable for personal sin. The narrative opens with the heavenly scene that reveals the ordeal allowed by God, passes to human lament and long debates between Job and his friends, and culminates in divine intervention, which does not offer the desired explanation, but confronts Job, corrects his perspective and confirms his faithfulness. The book does not intend to solve the riddle of suffering, but to show that pain is not an automatic proof of guilt and that human wisdom is limited before the sovereignty of God.
profile.setting: The work situates its history at the beginning of the patriarchal era, before Israel existed as a nation. The social framework combines wealth in herds and servants, priestly performance of the head of the family and references to nomadic peoples, traits compatible with the period of the patriarchs. Although the plot is set at this ancient time, the literary composition of the book seems to have occurred well later, possibly during the monarchy; the authorship, the exact date and even possible layers of editing remain uncertain.

structure.label: Prose prologue and proof of Job
structure.description: Heavenly scene, divine permission for Job's test and first reaction to the losses and affliction.

structure.label: Poetic dialogues with friends
structure.description: I regret that Job, three cycles of debate and confrontation between the retributive reading of friends and Job's insistence on his integrity.

structure.label: Hymn to Wisdom
structure.description: Poetic interlude who exalts God as the only source of true wisdom.

structure.label: Last defense of Job
structure.description: Job recalls his previous condition, reaffirms his righteousness and closes his human argumentation.

structure.label: Speaks of Elihu
structure.description: New interlocutor intervenes to renew the attempt to explain Job's suffering.

structure.label: Response of God
structure.description: The Lord confronts Job with questions that emphasize his power and his sovereignty, without providing the requested explanation.

structure.label: Disclos and restoration
structure.description: Job humbles himself, God restores him, reproves his friends and grants abundant blessings.

themes: Suffering from the righteous without known guilt
Limits of Human Wisdom before God
Criticism of simplistic explanations of retribution
Sovereignty and the Justice of God
Perseverance, reverence and worship amidst pain
readingKeys: Notice how the book alternates between prose and poetry, and how the celestial prologue guides all the reading of human debates.
Carefully compare the thesis of friends with Job's answer: both speak of divine justice, but disagree on how to apply it to concrete suffering.
Pay attention to the end: God does not explain the hidden motive of the test, but repositions Job before his greatness and then vindicates him.
profile.cautions: The source introduction deals with Job's historicity as possible and supported by biblical references, but recognizes that the date of composition, authorship and even the editorial process cannot be fixed with certainty. It is also important not to force the book to offer a complete explanation of suffering: the work itself rejects easy answers and maintains the mystery under divine sovereignty.

dossier.narratedEra: Ancient patriarchal age before Israel became a nation and before the law of Moses; the setting is of clans and pastoral wealth, with Job living outside of Israelite territory. The notes place this setting as prior to the monarchy and even the establishment of Israel as a national people.
dossier.compositionEra: The composition is presented as much later than the patriarchal setting. Tyndale notes that the book was probably composed during the monarchy, although there are much wider academic proposals, from the desert period until after exile. Matthew Henry also treats the book as very old in content, but says that it is not possible to fix the date or the author with certainty; he mentions traditions that attribute the essay to Moses, Elihu or another inspired writer, without stating this as certainty.

politics.title: Job out of Israel's political order
politics.detail: Job is described as non-Israeli, living before the birth of the nation and outside its later territory. This puts him in a world prior to Israel's political structures and prevents reading the book as if it were a dispute within Israeli national history.
politics.readingImpact: The discussion of suffering does not depend on institutions of Israel, but on a broader human and sapiential scene prior to national history.

politics.title: You know as nomadic looters
politics.detail: The notes claim that the Sabaeans, in Job's time, were sacking desert tribes, and not yet a relevant national power. The contrast with the later monarchic era is explained in the notes, when the Sabaeans already appear as important economic and political power.
politics.readingImpact: Job's losses come from local and mobile attacks, not from a war between large states; this reinforces the vulnerability of its prosperity and the speed of devastation.

politics.title: Chaldeans as Invaders and Non-consolidated Empire
politics.detail: The introduction Tyndale says that in Job's time, the Chaldeans were nomadic looters and not yet the political and economic strength that would be in the late monarchical phase. The note does not describe details of the Chaldean empire, only this temporal contrast.
politics.readingImpact: The reader should visualize an ancient, tribal and unstable scenario; the loss of goods by Chaldean attack should not be read as an already established empire event, but as an incursion of armed gangs.

politics.title: Conflict in the heavenly council
politics.detail: The notes describe a scenario of court or heavenly counsel in which Satan appears before God and is allowed to test Job. This is not a human government, but a dispute of sovereignty and accusation in the divine sphere, which structures the entire initial narrative.
politics.readingImpact: Job's suffering gains a judicial and theological dimension: the reader sees that the main question is not only human, but involves the integrity of God and the accusation of Satan.

politics.title: Monarchy as the Probable horizon of the essay
politics.detail: Tyndale claims that the composition probably occurred during the monarchy, when other materials of wisdom, such as Proverbs and Ecclesiastes, were being assembled. Matthew Henry, more cautiously, mentions that some thought of later Isaiah or prophets, but without certainty. The source does not fix a specific king or a specific kingdom for writing.
politics.readingImpact: This helps the reader to distinguish the narrated world from the writing time, realizing that the literary form can reflect a later stage of Israel's sapiential tradition.

customs.title: Pastoral Wealth based on flocks and servants
customs.detail: Job is portrayed as very rich in cattle, servants and possessions, similar to the patriarchs. The notes also note that the catalog of wealth is realistic for a rich man of that period.
customs.readingImpact: Job's prosperity is neither urban nor monetary in the modern sense; this shapes the reading of losses as total destruction of an ancient domestic economy.

customs.title: Job as priest of the house itself
customs.detail: The notes say Job acted as a priest of his family, a common practice before the law of Moses. He purified himself and offered sacrifices in behalf of the children, which is framed as a patriarchal custom.
customs.readingImpact: The reader sees Job exercising domestic spiritual leadership, showing that his piety is active, daily and prior to the Levitical cult.

customs.title: Ritual Purification Before Sacrifice
customs.detail: The note on Job 1:5 mentions washing and changing clothes as common forms of purification before offering sacrifices. This links Job's action to concrete gestures of ritual purity known in the Old Testament.
customs.readingImpact: Job's prayer and sacrifice are not improvised; the text presents him as an attentive person to holiness and ritual discipline.

customs.title: Meal, Feast and Moral Worries
customs.detail: The introduction presupposes banquets of the children in shifts, and Job cares about the possibility of having sinned. The note points out that Job understood that sinful attitudes in the heart already constitute sin, and that the word used as "blesing" works as euphemism for curse in the context of blasphemy.
customs.readingImpact: The family setting of repeated feasts shows an ancient aristocratic house, but it also exposes Job's fear that domestic joy could hide guilt before God.

customs.title: Visible mourning: tearing dresses and shaving the head
customs.detail: Upon receiving the news, Job tears the cloak and shaves the head; the note explains that they were common rites of the ancient Near East to express deep pain and shock, sometimes replacing auto-injury. He prostrates himself, not in despair, but in adoration.
customs.readingImpact: The gesture shows real lament without denying faith; Job's pain is culturally intelligible, but theologically oriented to worship.

customs.title: Antique money: kesitah and gifts of honor
customs.detail: Tyndale states that the money quoted in the book, kesitah, was used in the patriarchal period; in Job 42:11, the gifts given to Job are explained as gifts of honor and search for favor, not just financial assistance. Matthew Henry also reads these gifts as recognition and attempt to reconcile.
customs.readingImpact: The economy of the book is archaic and relational: money appears as a social sign and not as a modern abstract system.

language.title: Ambiguous opening form between history and parable
language.detail: The notes note that the initial phrase "Havia a man" can introduce both a parable and a historical narrative. This is part of the literary way of the book, without solving the issue of historicity alone.
language.readingImpact: The reader is led to follow the narrative with literary and theological attention, without reducing the text to mere chronicle or simple fiction.

language.title: Wisdom in proverbs, rhetorical questions and eloquence
language.detail: Tyndale's introduction describes the author as wise, skillful in the use of proverbs, rhetorical questions, and eloquent language. This explains why Job's speeches are dense and argumentative.
language.readingImpact: The book should be read as disputeful sapiential poetry, where the form matters to the content, and not as a simple prose of information.

language.title: Job's poetry and the parallels of the ancient Near East
language.detail: Tyndale gathers parallels with Canaanus, Egyptian and Babylonian texts, highlighting similarities of theme and form, but also decisive differences, such as Job's monotheism and his continued fidelity to the Lord. The comparison with the "Babylonic Theodicea" highlights the shared dialogic structure.
language.readingImpact: These parallels show that the book talks to the sapiential literature of the ancient world, but is also distinguished by its own theology.

language.title: Euphemmism of "a bless" to "amaldiçoar"
language.detail: The note in Job 1:5 explains that the Hebrew term literally translated by "a bless" is used as euphemism for "amaldiçoar" in contexts of blasphemy. The same phenomenon reappears in Job 1:11; 2:5; 2:9.
language.readingImpact: The reader perceives the irony of vocabulary and the gravity of the implicit threat: the problem is not only suffering, but the possibility of language against God.

language.title: Language of integrity and absolute non-perfectness
language.detail: The notes insist that Job was upright and just, but not without sin in the absolute sense. The distinction between integrity, relative moral innocence and total perfection is important for the reading of Job's and friends' speeches.
language.readingImpact: It is avoided to read Job's defense as an affirmation of impeccability; the point is that his suffering does not stem from specific guilt.

language.title: Metaphor of the "wall of protection" and the "word of wisdom"
language.detail: Tyndale highlights images such as the Protection Wallet around Job and, in Job 21, the reference to the "light of the wicked" that does not seem to be erased. Such images participate in the poetic argument of the discourses.
language.readingImpact: The images broaden the reading: protection, prosperity and apparent impunity are treated as visible realities, not just abstract ideas.

timeline.title: Patriarchal Time before Moses and the nation of Israel
timeline.detail: The setting is explicitly placed at the beginning of the patriarchal era. Job lives before Israel became a nation, before the Mosaic law and in a context similar to that of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
timeline.readingImpact: This guides the reading to the world of patriarchs: family, flocks, domestic priesthood and absence of national Israeli institutions.

timeline.title: Traditions of composition dating, but without certainty
timeline.detail: Tyndale summarizes proposals ranging from the desert period until after exile, while Matthew Henry mentions ancient traditions that attribute the work to Moses and conjectures over Elihu or other inspired authors. None of these hypotheses are presented as certain.
timeline.readingImpact: The reader must separate the date of the narrated events of the editorial history and not confuse a patriarchal scenario with the date of the writing.

timeline.title: Oldest mention of Job at the time of exile
timeline.detail: Tyndale's introduction states that the oldest biblical reference to Job appears in Ezekiel 14:14, 20, in exile. This is used as a minimum limit for the character's reception in Scripture.
timeline.readingImpact: It shows that Job was already known as an example of justice before the final fixation of the book in the canon, helping to understand his literary and moral authority.

timeline.title: Exceptionally long lifespan
timeline.detail: The notes note that Job lived 140 years after his restoration and that this fits into the patriarchal pattern of longevity, comparable to the biblical patriarchs. Matthew Henry also describes the book as belonging to a time when life expectancy was longer than that of Moses.
timeline.readingImpact: The internal chronology reinforces the old photo frame of the book and prevents anachronistic readings on family, inheritance and aging.

timeline.title: Restoration in four generations
timeline.detail: The note on Job 42:16 highlights that Job saw children, grandchildren and great-grandchildren, that is, four generations. Longevity functions as a sign of blessing restored within the logic of the book.
timeline.readingImpact: The story ends not only with renewed wealth, but with generational continuity, underlining the reversal of the initial loss.

investigation: The introduction Tyndale strongly supports the patriarchal setting, but also states that the composition is probably later and possibly editorially complex; Matthew Henry adds old conjectures about authorship, without solving the problem.

The sources do not identify a specific king, a dominant empire, or an exact chronology for the essay; they only contrast Job's world with later periods in which Sabaeans and Chaldeans would already be powers.
The parallels of the ancient Near East are presented as literary and thematic analogies, not as evidence of direct dependence or simple copying.
There is debate in its own notes on the relationship between history and poetry: the text is treated as true history in poetic form, but openness and dialogues maintain literary complexity.
Some observations about names, coins and customs are explanatory inferences of banknotes; they help in reading, but do not replace external historical evidence.
dossier.limits: This dossier uses only the provided notes and therefore depends on the selective coverage of them. The sections of politics and chronology are limited because the sources hardly deal with human rulers, empires or detachable events accurately; the focus lies on the patriarchal frame, nomadic looters and heavenly council. In customs, the explicitly mentioned items are concentrated: pastoral wealth, domestic priesthood, ritual purification, mourning, gifts and inheritance. In language, only resources were included actually discussed in the notes: literary form, proverbs, rhetorical questions, euphemism, old poetry and parallels. Where the source speaks of "probable," "looks" or "some thought," this was marked as interpretation or debate, without turning into historical certainty. No external data or speculative chronologies were introduced.
